title: Unmoved by pain
hookLine: jo nar dukh mai dukh nahee maanai: the one unmoved by pain, pleasure, praise, gold or dust (Sorath M9, ang 633)

lines: THE STUBBED TOE: THE FIRST PAIN.
cards: Stub your toe on the bed frame at night, and there are two pains. The first is the toe: sharp, real, over in a minute. The second arrives a moment later.
Why is the bed there? Why does this always happen to me? Everything's ruined.
The second pain can last for hours, and it's mostly made of words. A hymn of Guru Tegh Bahadur's in Raag Sorath begins with someone who feels the first pain, and doesn't add the second.

teach.b: The hymn opens jo nar dukh mai dukh nahee maanai. The one who, in pain, doesn't take pain as pain. Dukh is pain, sorrow.
Maanai is to accept, to take something as so. The line doesn't say this person feels nothing. It says that in the middle of dukh, they don't crown it king.
Then the hymn draws a portrait, in paraphrase. No clinging to pleasure, no fear.
Gold and dust seen alike. No slander, no flattery, no greed, attachment or pride. Apart from joy and grief, from honor and dishonor.
Lust and anger can't touch this person, and in that heart, the hymn says, God lives. Who can live like this? Only the one the Guru has blessed, it says, understands the way.
And the last line is a picture: Nanak has merged with the Lord, like water with water. Pour water into water, and there's no seam, nothing to defend. That's the inner reason for the steadiness.
The one who is level in all weather isn't gritting their teeth. They've stopped holding themselves apart. And this isn't coldness.
Sikh teaching calls for service, sharing and standing up for others, and Sikhs remember the ninth Guru as giving his life to defend other people's freedom of faith.
This steadiness is the calm that lets you act well in a storm, instead of being thrown around by it.

how: Guru Tegh Bahadur's Sorath shabad 'jo nar dukh mai dukh nahee maanai' is sung in kirtan, and Sikhs often recall its portrait of steadiness in times of grief or illness.

o: pain or sorrow, in body or mind
fear of what might still come

games.q: unmoved by pain — tap the pairs.

s: the hymn says the steady person feels nothing at all
in pain, they don't take pain as pain; they feel it without crowning it king.
the hymn says that in such a heart, God lives
lust and anger can't touch that person, and in that heart God dwells.
the steadiness here means not caring about others
it's the calm that lets you serve well in a storm.

games.q: you stub your toe in the dark, and the mind starts a long story about how everything is ruined. what does the Sorath hymn describe?
o: feeling the pain without taking it as the whole truth.
getting angry at whoever moved the bed.
games.why: jo nar dukh mai dukh nahee maanai: in pain, they don't take pain as pain. the hymn ends with Nanak merged with the Lord like water with water.

practice: Check in with whatever mood is here, restless, low, cheerful, tired, and feel it the way you'd feel weather on your face, without changing it.

When the story about the mood starts, I shouldn't feel this, this will last forever, come back to the breath and let the mood pass over a steady field. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths.

wordCard.voice: Dukh, pain or sorrow. In Guru Tegh Bahadur's Sorath hymn, the one who doesn't take it as pain is level through every weather, merged with the Lord like water with water.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: dukh, pain or sorrow, the first word of the hymn's portrait.

carryVoice: Your line: level in all weather. The first pain is real; the second is mostly words. More tomorrow.

sources.ref: Raag Sorath, Mahalla 9, 'jo nar dukh mai dukh nahee maanai' (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 633–634)
